instruments.name: Camera
instruments.measures: Colour, shape, texture and layering, seen as an image.
instruments.why: Scientists look first: colour and texture suggest what a rock might be and where to look more closely.
instruments.real: Inspired by the Panoramic Camera (Pancam) on NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers.

instruments.name: Spectrometer
instruments.measures: Which chemical elements and minerals are present (shown here as simulated indicators).
instruments.why: Composition is evidence a picture cannot give: two rocks can look alike but be made of different things.
instruments.real: Inspired by the Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer and Mössbauer spectrometer carried by Spirit and Opportunity.

instruments.name: Microscope
instruments.measures: Grain size, grain shape and surface structure, close up.
instruments.why: Grain size and texture tell how a rock or soil formed: cooled lava, smashed fragments, wind-blown sand or water-laid layers.
instruments.real: Inspired by the Microscopic Imager on Spirit and Opportunity.

instruments.name: Magnetic sensor
instruments.measures: How strongly the sample responds to a magnet (simulated).
instruments.why: Magnetic response hints at iron-bearing minerals and helps compare materials.
instruments.real: Inspired by the magnets on the Viking 1 lander, whose goals included the magnetic properties of the Martian surface, the magnet array on Spirit, and the portable magnetometer carried on Apollo 16.

moon.name: Lunar Exploration Mission
moon.intro: Your rover has landed on a fictional lunar plain beside the bright highlands. Find deposits, collect samples, and let the evidence tell you what happened here.
objectives: Analyse each with at least 2 instruments
Answer the reasoning challenge for 2 samples

mars.name: Martian Exploration Mission
mars.intro: Your rover is on a fictional Martian plain with dunes, outcrops and dust. Collect samples and decide which conclusions the evidence really supports.
objectives: Analyse each with at least 2 instruments
Answer the reasoning challenge for 2 samples

mare_basalt.name: Dark volcanic rock
mare_basalt.label: Dark rock from the plain

camera.Texture: Massive, fine-grained; a few small holes

microscope.Structure: Interlocking crystals, as in cooled lava

mare_basalt.interpretation: A mare basalt: volcanic lava that flooded the dark lunar plains. The maria are dark, low-lying lava plains; high-titanium mare basalts contain about 9–13% titanium dioxide.
mare_basalt.uncertainty: These instruments cannot date the rock. NASA's sample guide gives returned mare basalts ages of about 3.15–3.85 billion years, but those ages came from laboratory measurements on Earth.

questions.q: What do the high iron and elevated titanium indications suggest?
options: It is a basalt like those that flooded the lunar maria
It is a piece of ice
questions.best: It is a basalt like those that flooded the lunar maria
questions.explain: Iron- and titanium-rich, finely crystalline dark rock matches the mare basalts. NASA's sample guide describes high-Ti mare basalts with about 9–13% titanium dioxide.

questions.q: Could this sample alone prove how old the lunar plains are?
options: Yes, its colour shows its age
questions.best: No: age needs laboratory dating
questions.explain: Colour, composition and texture do not give an age. Mare basalt ages (about 3.15–3.85 billion years in NASA's sample guide) come from laboratory measurements on returned samples.

anorthosite.name: Bright highland rock
anorthosite.label: Bright rock from the highland edge

microscope.Structure: Large pale crystals, fractured by impacts

anorthosite.interpretation: An anorthosite from the lunar highlands, the ancient crust. Lunar anorthosites are called ferroan anorthosites; NASA's guide notes that highland samples have all been through several cratering events.
anorthosite.uncertainty: The crushed texture shows impact damage, which makes it hard to know how much of the original rock is unaltered.

questions.q: The sample is bright and rich in calcium and aluminium, with little iron. What does that suggest?
questions.best: Highland crust rock (anorthosite)
questions.explain: Bright, calcium- and aluminium-rich rock dominated by plagioclase matches lunar highland anorthosite, part of the early crust.

questions.q: The crystals are fractured. Which conclusion does the evidence support best?
options: The rock has been damaged by impacts
questions.best: The rock has been damaged by impacts
questions.explain: NASA's guide notes that all highland samples have undergone several cratering events, so fractured crystals fit impact damage. Nothing here points to water.

breccia.name: Fragment-filled rock
breccia.label: Rock made of broken pieces

camera.Colour: Mixed grey, light and dark patches
camera.Texture: Angular fragments set in a finer matrix

spectrometer.Composition: Mixed: varies from fragment to fragment

microscope.Grain size: Very mixed: fine matrix with large clasts

breccia.interpretation: An impact breccia. NASA describes lunar breccias as the lithified aggregates of clastic debris and melt generated by meteorite bombardment; most Apollo breccias formed in the highlands about 3.9–4.0 billion years ago.
breccia.uncertainty: Each fragment may come from a different source rock, so the whole sample does not tell one simple story.

questions.q: What process most likely formed this rock?
options: Meteorite impacts smashed and welded fragments together
Slow cooling of a single lava flow
questions.best: Meteorite impacts smashed and welded fragments together
questions.explain: Angular clasts in a fine matrix with melt are the signature of impact breccias, formed by meteorite bombardment.

questions.q: What additional measurement would best show where the fragments came from?
options: Analyse the composition of individual fragments
questions.best: Analyse the composition of individual fragments
questions.explain: Because each clast can be a different rock, scientists analyse fragments separately to trace their sources.

regolith.name: Fine grey soil
regolith.label: Loose grey soil

spectrometer.Other indicators: Implanted hydrogen and helium from the solar wind (simulated)

microscope.Grain size: Very fine: much of it smaller than a tenth of a millimetre
microscope.Structure: Irregular glassy clumps (agglutinates) among rock and mineral grains

regolith.interpretation: Lunar regolith: the layer of loose debris covering the Moon. NASA's guide describes it as a fine grey soil, about half of which is smaller than 60–80 microns. Micrometeorites melt parts of it into agglutinates, and the solar wind implants hydrogen and helium.
regolith.uncertainty: Regolith is constantly reworked by micrometeorites, so its grains have mixed histories.

questions.q: The microscope shows glassy clumps. What made them?
questions.best: Micrometeorite impacts melting the soil
questions.explain: With no atmosphere, the Moon's surface is bombarded by micrometeorites that melt soil into agglutinates.

questions.q: Does finding hydrogen in this soil prove there was once liquid water here?
options: No: the solar wind implants hydrogen into lunar soil
questions.best: No: the solar wind implants hydrogen into lunar soil
questions.explain: NASA's guide explains that the solar wind implants hydrogen and helium into the soil. Hydrogen alone is not evidence of past liquid water.

orange_glass.name: Orange soil
orange_glass.label: Unusual orange patch
orange_glass.interpretation: Volcanic glass beads, like the orange soil Harrison Schmitt discovered on Apollo 17. NASA reports that analysis showed it to be small spherical glass beads with a high titanium content. NASA's sample guide suggests orange glass may be the cause of the dark mantle at the edge of Mare Serenitatis.
orange_glass.uncertainty: Colour alone could mislead; the evidence that matters is the bead shape and the composition.

questions.q: The sample is made of tiny glass spheres. Which explanation fits the evidence best?
options: Molten droplets that cooled quickly, as in a volcanic eruption
questions.best: Molten droplets that cooled quickly, as in a volcanic eruption
questions.explain: Glass forms when melt cools too fast to crystallise, and spherical beads point to droplets. Apollo 17's orange soil turned out to be volcanic glass beads.

questions.q: Is the bright orange colour enough on its own to identify the material?
options: Yes, orange always means volcanic glass
No: you also need shape and composition evidence
questions.best: No: you also need shape and composition evidence
questions.explain: Colour is a clue, not proof. The microscope (bead shape) and spectrometer (high titanium) provide the supporting evidence.

olivine_basalt.name: Dark volcanic rock
olivine_basalt.label: Dark rock, dusty surface

camera.Colour: Dark grey under a reddish dust coating
camera.Texture: Fine-grained, with a thin surface coating

microscope.Structure: Crystalline volcanic texture; thin coatings and vein fillings at the surface

olivine_basalt.interpretation: An olivine-bearing basalt, like the rocks under Spirit's landing plain in Gusev Crater. NASA's mission overview notes that those plains rocks are covered by wind-blown dust, and that their coatings and vein fillings record a minor amount of transport and deposition by water.
olivine_basalt.uncertainty: A thin coating could hide or change what the rock's surface tells you; real rovers brush or grind rocks before analysing them.

questions.q: What does the olivine indication suggest about this rock?
questions.best: It is a volcanic basalt
questions.explain: Olivine-bearing, finely crystalline dark rock matches the olivine basalts Spirit studied in Gusev Crater.

questions.q: Do the thin coatings prove that a large lake once covered this rock?
options: No: they suggest at most a small amount of water activity
questions.best: No: they suggest at most a small amount of water activity
questions.explain: NASA's overview describes only a minor amount of transport and deposition by water at Gusev's plains. Coatings alone cannot prove a lake.

hematite_spherules.name: Grey spherules
hematite_spherules.label: Field of tiny grey spheres

camera.Texture: Many small round spheres scattered on the surface

microscope.Grain size: Small spheres, much larger than the surrounding dust
microscope.Structure: Round, resistant grains; some still embedded in layered rock

hematite_spherules.interpretation: Hematite spherules, like Opportunity's "blueberries" at Meridiani Planum. NASA notes that on Earth gray crystalline hematite forms mostly in association with liquid water, and that Opportunity's spherules formed late from rising, acidic groundwater.
hematite_spherules.uncertainty: Hematite can form in more than one way, so scientists combine composition with the setting: the spheres were embedded in layered sedimentary rock.

questions.q: Could this sample provide evidence of past water activity?
options: Yes: gray hematite spherules like these are linked to groundwater
No: hematite has nothing to do with water
questions.best: Yes: gray hematite spherules like these are linked to groundwater
questions.explain: On Earth, gray crystalline hematite forms mostly with liquid water, and NASA reports that Opportunity's blueberries formed from rising, acidic groundwater.

questions.q: What additional observation would most strengthen the water interpretation?
options: Finding the spheres embedded in water-laid layered rock
questions.best: Finding the spheres embedded in water-laid layered rock
questions.explain: Context matters. At Meridiani the blueberries were embedded in soft, layered sedimentary sandstone, which strengthened the water story.

layered_sandstone.name: Layered outcrop
layered_sandstone.label: Pale, finely layered rock

camera.Texture: Thin layers; soft and easily eroded

spectrometer.Indicated minerals: Sulfate salts mixed with altered sand grains (simulated)

layered_sandstone.interpretation: A sedimentary sandstone. NASA reports that Opportunity was the first rover to identify and characterize sedimentary rocks on another planet, and that its measurements showed these rocks formed in ancient ephemeral playas: shallow, temporary bodies of water.
layered_sandstone.uncertainty: Layering alone could also come from wind. Composition and context are needed to separate wind-laid from water-laid layers.

questions.q: The rock is layered and sulfur-rich. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: It formed where water came and went, like a temporary playa
It is a fresh lava flow
questions.best: It formed where water came and went, like a temporary playa
questions.explain: NASA reports that Opportunity's layered sedimentary rocks formed in ancient ephemeral playas. Salt-rich layers fit evaporating water.

questions.q: If you only had the camera image, could you be sure water laid these layers?
options: No: wind can also make layers
questions.best: No: wind can also make layers
questions.explain: Layers are an observation; "water" is an interpretation. Composition and grain evidence are needed before concluding.

red_dust.name: Red dust and soil
red_dust.label: Reddish dusty soil

camera.Texture: Very fine dust over coarser soil

microscope.Grain size: Very fine dust; some sand grains

red_dust.interpretation: Martian dust and soil. NASA explains that Mars looks red because iron minerals in the Martian dirt oxidize, or rust.
red_dust.uncertainty: Dust is carried by wind across the planet, so it may not come from the rock directly below it.

questions.q: Why is this soil red?
questions.best: Its iron minerals have oxidised (rusted)
questions.explain: NASA: iron minerals in the Martian dirt oxidize, or rust, causing the surface to look red.

questions.q: Can you be sure this dust came from the rock directly underneath?
options: Yes, dust always comes from below
No: wind moves dust across Mars
questions.best: No: wind moves dust across Mars
questions.explain: Wind carries dust long distances, so its source is uncertain without more evidence.

gypsum_vein.name: White mineral vein
gypsum_vein.label: Bright white line in the rock

camera.Texture: Thin vein filling a crack in darker rock

gypsum_vein.interpretation: A gypsum vein, like the white veins Opportunity found on the rim of Endeavour crater. NASA calls gypsum veins a telltale sign of water that travelled through underground fractures.
gypsum_vein.uncertainty: A vein shows that water moved through the rock, but not how long ago or whether the water was ever on the surface.

questions.q: What does a calcium-sulfate (gypsum) vein filling a crack suggest?
questions.best: Water flowed through underground fractures
questions.explain: NASA describes Opportunity's gypsum veins as a telltale sign of water that travelled through underground fractures.

questions.q: Does this vein show that Mars had surface lakes at the same time?
options: No: it shows underground water, not surface lakes
questions.best: No: it shows underground water, not surface lakes
questions.explain: A vein records groundwater moving through cracks. Surface lakes would need other evidence.
